newsitem.title: CANADA: Getting Fido to fetch the digital news album.
newsitem.headline: Getting Fido to fetch the digital news album.

text.p: The newspapers still arrive with a thud outside the door in the wee hours of the morning but somehow the excitement of getting up and reading the printed word has lost some of its luster of late.

Could it be the romance with the old broadsheets of information has faded with the arrival of another love interest? Could it be that all those Internet news services parading around with their out-of-this-world graphics, videos and sound are starting to attract interest?

There are a number of amazing news sites and electronic magazines on the World Wide Web. What they do compared with your old stodgy newspaper is pretty incredible. The phrase "read all about it" is really passe when you can read, view and hear the news on the Net.

Senior news executives will tell you privately they have plans to substantially boost the use of video and other exciting multimedia applications at their sites, as soon as the bandwidth is more widely available to allow it all.

However, one also hears undercurrents that big content providers have trouble getting surfers to come back. Often people will pay for a news serivce on the Web but don't return regularly, which makes life difficult for service providers at subscription renewal time.

Perhaps the problem is that electronic newspapers are just not user-friendly. It's not much fun taking your desktop boat anchor or your slab top computer to your favorite chair, into the bathtub or on to the subway.
But if news read on regurgitated dead trees is not too exciting anymore, then maybe we have to invent something entirely new.
How about instead of trying to stuff newspapers into computer boxes, we consider stuffing computers into newspapers?

Imagine a device like a photo album with strong outer coverings and thin but sturdy pages. The pages and the cover could be embedded with computer chips programmed to display numerous stories and headlines. Other chips would run videos or pictures in areas with built-in liquid display screens. Sound bites could be delivered via razor-thin speakers on the inside covers of the album.

Unlike newspapers, this news album would be reusable. The device could be plugged into a docking station each night to receive a host news goodies, features, video clips, pictures and the like over the Net. It would be programmable where readers could choose a mix of local, national and international news to fit their tastes.

Of course, the album would include advertising and some kind of subscription fee would doubtless be needed to underwrite the heavy upfront hardware costs. But imagine how news organizations could bulldoze printing presses and instead use low cost manufacturers to turn out the electronic news albums.
Each morning the news album could be thrown into a brief case and read on planes, trains and automobiles. It could become a handy, handsome unit that news fans would love to read daily.

Most importantly, it would have to be easy to use with the comfortable feel of a book or newspaper where the reader could leisurely flip pages while taking in a world of information, sounds and sights.
An outlandish idea because of technical or economical constraints?
Perhaps, but it seems we would benefit from some kind of a conjugal arrangement between these two imprisoned technologies to render a more superior creation for our rabid news-reading desires.
